summary: Talha Sheikh opens by describing a common frustration: Claude Code claims a task is complete, but when the user runs the code, things fail, requiring repeated manual corrections. He identifies himself as the enforcement layer—constantly telling the agent what to fix. To solve this, he built Vector V1, a product that deterministically checks Claude's output via Claude hooks. When a session ends, the hook calls Vector, runs defined test cases, and if checks fail, tells Claude to retry until all pass. This shifts the question from 'can the agent do the task?' to 'can I trust it did the task correctly?' An Anthropic engineer told him enforcement wouldn't be needed once smarter models arrived, triggering a crisis. Sheikh reasoned through it by distinguishing capability from reliability: more capable models are not automatically more reliable. Good instructions and context are not the same as verification. He also noted that with strong guardrails, smaller or open-source models can be used, reducing cost. After speaking at events, he realized everyone (Anthropic, Meta, his own company) builds their own enforcement, so the solution must be a shareable, language-agnostic pattern or contract. It should run at every stage—conversations, pre-commit, multi-agent workflows, async operations, and LLM-as-judge checks. He cites converging industry examples: Anthropic's advisor pattern, OpenAI's harness engineering, Codo's comprehensive code reviews, and a Work OS principle to 'enforce, don't instruct.' His closing message: the value has shifted from the code produced to the verification designed, so work on the harness, not the code.

sections.title: Problem: The Human as Enforcement Layer
sections.summary: Sheikh describes giving Claude Code a task, seeing it complete, but finding failures at runtime that require repeated manual fixes. He identifies the user as the enforcement layer who must check the agent's work every time.

sections.title: Building Vector V1 with Claude Hooks
sections.summary: He built Vector V1 to deterministically check Claude's output via hooks that fire after a session ends. A config file defines test cases; failures trigger retries to Claude until all checks pass.

sections.title: Crisis: Smarter Models Won't Need Enforcement?
sections.summary: An Anthropic engineer told him future models would be so smart enforcement wouldn't be needed. Sheikh questioned whether he wasted his time, then distinguished capability from reliability.

sections.title: Capability vs Reliability and Cost Reduction
sections.summary: More capability doesn't mean more reliability. Good instructions are not verification. With guardrails, smaller models like Haiku or open-source models can be used, reducing cost; more harness investment reduces cost drastically.

sections.title: From Product to Shareable Pattern
sections.summary: After talking to more people, Sheikh realized everyone builds their own enforcement. The solution must be a language-agnostic, shareable pattern—a contract that runs at every stage: conversations, commits, multi-agent workflows, async tasks, and LLM-as-judge.

sections.title: Industry Convergence on Verification
sections.summary: He cites Anthropic's advisor pattern, OpenAI's harness engineering, Codo's comprehensive code reviews, and Work OS's 'enforce, don't instruct' principle. All converge on deterministic verification as essential.

sections.title: TLDR and Q&A
sections.summary: Value has shifted from code produced to verification designed. Work on the harness, not the code. Q&A confirms Vector Harness is public and available via LinkedIn.
